paper_profile.title: Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors
paper_profile.abstract: Memory isolation is a key property of a reliable and secure computing system — an access to one memory address should not have unintended side effects on data stored in other addresses. However, as DRAM process technology scales down to smaller dimensions, it becomes more difficult to prevent DRAM cells from electrically interacting with each other. In this paper, we expose the vulnerability of commodity DRAM chips to disturbance errors. By reading from the same address in DRAM, we show that it is possible to corrupt data in nearby addresses. More specifically, activating the same row in DRAM corrupts data in nearby rows. We demonstrate this phenomenon on Intel and AMD systems using a malicious program that generates many DRAM accesses. We induce errors in most DRAM modules (110 out of 129) from three major DRAM manufacturers. From this we conclude that many deployed systems are likely to be at risk. We identify the root cause of disturbance errors as the repeated toggling of a DRAM row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. We provide an extensive characterization study of disturbance errors and their behavior using an FPGA-based testing platform. Among our key findings, we show that (i) it takes as few as 139K accesses to induce an error and (ii) up to one in every 1.7K cells is susceptible to errors. After examining various potential ways of addressing the problem, we propose a low-overhead solution to prevent the errors.
paper_profile.research_problem: The paper investigates DRAM disturbance errors, a phenomenon where repeatedly activating (opening/closing) the same DRAM row corrupts data stored in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. It aims to expose the widespread existence of these errors in commodity DRAM chips, characterize their behavior, identify their root cause, and propose a low-overhead solution to prevent them.

paper_profile.summary: This paper exposes and characterizes DRAM disturbance errors (the "row hammer" phenomenon), where repeatedly activating the same DRAM row corrupts data in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. The authors demonstrate the phenomenon on real Intel (Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell) and AMD (Piledriver) systems using a user-level program that continuously reads from DRAM, inducing thousands of bit-flips. They identify the root cause as repeated toggling of a row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. Using an FPGA-based testing platform, they characterize 129 DDR3 DRAM modules (972 chips) from three major manufacturers, finding disturbance errors in 110 modules (836 chips), with all modules manufactured in 2012-2013 being vulnerable. Key findings include: it takes as few as 139K activations to induce an error, up to one in 1.7K cells is susceptible, victim cells are predominantly localized to the two immediately adjacent rows, errors affect only charged cells (causing them to discharge), and errors are mostly repeatable but not strongly correlated with weak cells or temperature. The paper examines six potential solutions (better chips, ECC, frequent refreshes, cell retirement by manufacturer or end-user, and hot-row detection) and finds them all limited. It then proposes PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation), a stateless low-overhead mechanism where each time a row is opened/closed, an adjacent row is refreshed with low probability p. PARA provides a strong statistical guarantee against disturbance errors (error probability as low as 9.4e-14 over one year with p=0.001 and Nth=100K) while incurring only 0.197% average performance degradation across 29 benchmarks.

paper_profile.title: Paxos Made Live - An Engineering Perspective
paper_profile.abstract: We describe our experience in building a fault-tolerant database using the Paxos consensus algorithm. Despite the existing literature in the field, building such a database proved to be non-trivial. We describe selected algorithmic and engineering problems encountered, and the solutions we found for them. Our measurements indicate that we have built a competitive system.
paper_profile.research_problem: The paper addresses the practical challenges of moving the Paxos consensus algorithm from theory to a production-ready fault-tolerant database, including algorithmic gaps in the literature, software engineering challenges, and unexpected real-world failures.

paper_profile.summary: This paper describes the engineering experience of building a production fault-tolerant database at Google based on the Paxos consensus algorithm, used to replace the commercial third-party database (3DB) underlying the Chubby lock service. The authors detail the architecture, where a fault-tolerant replicated log based on Paxos sits at the bottom of the protocol stack, with a fault-tolerant replicated database on top, and Chubby using that database. They describe algorithmic challenges and solutions: handling disk corruption (via checksums, GFS markers, and non-voting rebuild), master leases to serve reads locally, epoch numbers to detect master turnover, group membership changes, snapshots with snapshot handles, and the MultiOp primitive providing atomic transaction-style support. They also discuss software engineering methods including a state machine specification language compiled to C++, runtime consistency checking via periodic checksums, and repeatable randomized failure-injection testing in safety and liveness modes. The paper documents unexpected production failures over 100+ machine years, including thread starvation causing master failover cascades, upgrade script failures causing data loss, semantic mismatches between database and Chubby, memory corruption, and OS bugs. Performance measurements show the Paxos-based system outperforms 3DB by 1.2x to 4.4x across various workloads. The authors conclude that significant gaps remain between Paxos theory and practice, and argue the fault-tolerance community should develop better tools and testing approaches, drawing a comparison to the compiler construction field.

paper_profile.title: Processing in Storage Class Memory
paper_profile.abstract: Storage and memory technologies are experiencing unprecedented transformation. Storage-class memory (SCM) delivers near-DRAM performance in non-volatile storage media and became commercially available in 2019. Unfortunately, software is not yet able to fully benefit from such high-performance storage. Processing-in-memory (PIM) aims to overcome the notorious memory wall; at the time of writing, hardware is close to being commercially available. This paper takes a position that PIM will become an integral part of future storage-class memories, so data processing can be performed in-storage, saving memory bandwidth and CPU cycles. Under that assumption, we identify typical data-processing tasks poised for in-storage processing, such as compression, encryption and format conversion. We present evidence supporting our assumption and present some feasibility experiments on new PIM hardware to show the potential.
paper_profile.research_problem: The paper addresses the scalability problem in the storage subsystem, where CPU cycles and memory bandwidth become bottlenecks as storage performance increases. It proposes using Processing-in-Memory (PIM) processors integrated with Storage Class Memory (SCM) to offload simple data-processing tasks (e.g., compression, encryption, format conversion) from the host CPU to in-storage processors.

paper_profile.summary: This position paper argues that Processing-in-Memory (PIM) will become an integral part of future Storage Class Memory (SCM) systems, enabling data processing to be performed in-storage to save memory bandwidth and CPU cycles. The authors identify typical data-processing tasks suited for in-storage processing, including compression, encryption, and format conversion. They describe the UPMEM PIM hardware architecture (Data Processing Units embedded in DRAM) as a proxy for future PIM on SCM, discussing design considerations such as inter-PIM communication, address translation, core density, and instruction set. They propose a wishlist for future PIM architectures including data triggered functions, concurrent memory access, mixing of memory types, and performance tuning. Feasibility experiments show that format parsing overhead is higher relative to total time on NVRAM (42%) than on HDD (13%), and that compression overhead is higher on NVRAM than HDD for 17 of 35 benchmark operations. A Snappy decompression implementation on PIM hardware achieved a speedup of nearly 4.5x with the largest file using 172 DPUs, and a throughput measurement showed approximately 252 GB/sec, more than 13x the theoretical bandwidth of a single DDR4-2400 channel. The paper concludes that PIM on SCM is a promising direction for offloading simple tasks to free CPU cycles and memory bus cycles.

paper_profile.title: B4: Experience with a Globally-Deployed Software Defined WAN
paper_profile.abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of B4, a private WAN connecting Google's data centers across the planet. B4 has a number of unique characteristics: i) massive bandwidth requirements deployed to a modest number of sites, ii) elastic traffic demand that seeks to maximize average bandwidth, and iii) full control over the edge servers and network, which enables rate limiting and demand measurement at the edge. These characteristics led to a Software Defined Networking architecture using OpenFlow to control relatively simple switches built from merchant silicon. B4's centralized traffic engineering service drives links to near 100% utilization, while splitting application flows among multiple paths to balance capacity against application priority/demands. We describe experience with three years of B4 production deployment, lessons learned, and areas for future work.

paper_profile.summary: This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of B4, Google's private Software Defined WAN connecting its data centers worldwide. B4 was motivated by unique characteristics: massive bandwidth requirements across a modest number of sites, elastic traffic demand seeking to maximize average bandwidth, and full control over edge servers and network enabling rate limiting and demand measurement at the edge. These led to an SDN architecture using OpenFlow to control relatively simple switches built from merchant silicon. The architecture has three layers: switch hardware, site controllers (Network Control Servers hosting OpenFlow controllers and Network Control Applications), and a global layer with logically centralized applications (SDN Gateway and central TE server). B4 integrates existing routing protocols (BGP/ISIS via Quagga) with OpenFlow-based switch control through a Routing Application Proxy, enabling hybrid deployments and a gradual rollout. The centralized traffic engineering service allocates bandwidth among competing applications using max-min fair allocation, with bandwidth functions capturing relative application priority. The TE optimization algorithm (Tunnel Group Generation and Tunnel Group Quantization) achieves similar fairness and at least 99% of LP bandwidth utilization with 25x faster performance. TE drives links to near 100% utilization while splitting flows among multiple paths. B4 has been in production for three years, carries more traffic than Google's public facing WAN, and achieves 2-3x efficiency improvements over standard practice. The paper reports on deployment evolution, TE operations performance, failure impact, link utilization and hashing effectiveness, and lessons from a substantial outage. Key findings include near-100% link utilization, 14% average throughput improvement over shortest-path routing, hitless OFC/TE server failovers, and challenges in the OFC-OFA packet IO path and hardware programming overheads. The paper concludes that while the architecture does not generalize to all SDNs or WANs, the hybrid approach of supporting existing routing protocols alongside novel TE services demonstrates an effective technique for gradually introducing SDN into existing deployments.

paper_profile.title: Collection Tree Protocol
paper_profile.abstract: This paper presents and evaluates two principles for wireless routing protocols. The first is datapath validation: data traffic quickly discovers and fixes routing inconsistencies. The second is adaptive beaconing: extending the Trickle algorithm to routing control traffic reduces route repair latency and sends fewer beacons. We evaluate datapath validation and adaptive beaconing in CTP Noe, a sensor network tree collection protocol. We use 12 different testbeds ranging in size from 20–310 nodes, comprising seven platforms, and six different link layers, on both interference-free and interference-prone channels. In all cases, CTP Noe delivers > 90% of packets. Many experiments achieve 99.9%. Compared to standard beaconing, CTP Noe sends 73% fewer beacons while reducing topology repair latency by 99.8%. Finally, when using low-power link layers, CTP Noe has duty cycles of 3% while supporting aggregate loads of 30 packets/minute.
paper_profile.research_problem: How to design a wireless sensor network collection routing protocol that remains efficient, robust, and reliable in the presence of highly dynamic link topologies, addressing the challenges of link dynamics and transient loops.
methods: Adaptive beaconing (extension of the Trickle algorithm)
main_contributions: Describes two key principles, adaptive beaconing and datapath validation, which enable routing layers to remain efficient, robust, and reliable in highly dynamic topologies on many different link layers.
Describes the design and implementation of CTP Noe, a collection protocol that uses these two mechanisms.
Provides a comparative study of 12 different testbeds' behavior and properties, suggesting that protocols evaluated on only a single testbed are prone to failures under different network conditions.
claimed_innovations: Datapath validation: using data packets to actively validate the routing topology and detect loops, with each data packet containing the link-layer transmitter's estimate of its distance.

Adaptive beaconing: extending the Trickle algorithm to routing control traffic, allowing reaction in tens of milliseconds to topology changes while sending few control packets per hour when the topology is stable.
Using the routing cost gradient (rather than a global sequence number) to control when to reset the Trickle timer interval.
experimental_results: Across all testbeds, configurations, and CSMA layers, CTP Noe's end-to-end delivery ratio ranges from 90.5% to 99.9%.
CTP Noe supports median duty cycles of 3% while sustaining aggregate loads of 30 pkts per minute.

Compared to MultihopLQI's fixed 30 second beacon interval, CTP Noe's adaptive beaconing and datapath validation sends 73% fewer beacons while cutting loop recovery latency by 99.8%.
CTP Noe's delivery cost is 24% lower than MultihopLQI, with control packets occupying 2.2% of cost vs. 8.4% for MultihopLQI.
In a node-failure experiment, CTP Noe's minimum delivery ratio dropped only to 98%, while MultihopLQI's median delivery dropped to 80% for 10 minutes.
CTP Noe switched to a new parent in 325ms (12 packet transmissions) after its parent was removed, despite a beacon rate of one beacon every eight minutes.
The transmit cache improves CTP Noe's efficiency by 9% (cost from 3.47 to 3.18 packets/delivery).
On channel 16 (interference-prone), CTP Noe achieved 95.2% delivery vs. 99.9% on channel 26 (interference-free).
The full CTP Noe stack can run for as little as 7.2 mAh/day compared to 60.8 mAh/day for MultihopLQI on the Blaze platform.
In 6.5 hours, nodes sent 12,299 total beacons, detected 3,025 inconsistencies, and triggered 4,485 beacons due to parent change (2.6 beacons per inconsistency).
limitations: CTP Noe does not provide end-to-end reliability; transmit timers are insufficient for end-to-end reliability as bottleneck links of low PRR can overflow transmit queues, requiring higher-layer congestion and flow control.

The low-power probing vs. low-power listening comparison should not be interpreted as a general comparison of the two, as each implementation can be improved, CTP Noe is only one traffic pattern, and they were compared on a single testbed with a single traffic rate.
The testbeds are not field deployments, though they comprise diverse environmental conditions.
An open question is whether the techniques are general to distance vector algorithms and may have broader applicability in ad-hoc networking.
paper_profile.summary: This paper presents and evaluates two principles for wireless routing protocol design: datapath validation and adaptive beaconing, implemented in CTP Noe, an implementation of the Collection Tree Protocol (CTP) for wireless sensor networks. Datapath validation uses data packets to actively validate the routing topology and detect loops by having each data packet carry the transmitter's distance estimate, allowing detection of routing inconsistencies precisely when a route is needed. Adaptive beaconing extends the Trickle algorithm to routing control traffic, dynamically adapting the beacon interval between 64ms and one hour, resetting to the minimum on three events: forwarding a packet from a node with non-higher ETX, a significant cost decrease, or receiving a packet with the pull bit set. CTP Noe also includes data plane mechanisms: per-client queuing, a hybrid send queue, a transmit timer to avoid self-interference, and a transmit cache for duplicate suppression. The protocol is evaluated on 12 testbeds (20-310 nodes, seven platforms, six link layers) on both interference-free and interference-prone channels. Results show CTP Noe delivers over 90% of packets in all cases (many achieving 99.9%), sends 73% fewer beacons than MultihopLQI while reducing loop recovery latency by 99.8%, drops 90% fewer packets while sending 29% fewer packets, and achieves duty cycles of 3% while supporting aggregate loads of 30 packets/minute. The paper concludes that the efficacy of these techniques suggests wireless protocol limitations may be addressed by judiciously integrating data and control planes.

paper_profile.title: Remote Memory Calls
paper_profile.abstract: In this paper we propose an extension to RDMA, called Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), that allows applications to install a customized set of 1-sided RDMA operations. We then explain how RMCs can be implemented on the forthcoming generation of SmartNICs and discuss the resulting tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided RDMA operations, and 2-sided RDMA operations.
paper_profile.research_problem: The paper addresses the gap between the narrow set of 1-sided RDMA operations implemented in NIC hardware and the broader, more complex memory access patterns required by real distributed applications, which currently forces applications to either use inflexible 1-sided operations or CPU-expensive 2-sided operations.
methods: Modeling of latencies for linked list scan and remote buffer hashing workloads
Microbenchmark comparing RDMA read throughput between NIC-Host and Host-Host

Explains how RMCs can be implemented on forthcoming CPU-based SmartNICs

Discusses tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided RDMA operations, and 2-sided RDMA operations
Demonstrates benefits of RMCs through modeling of linked list scanning and remote buffer hashing workloads

RMCs as an abstraction that can be executed at the server SmartNIC, server CPU, client SmartNIC, or client CPU, enabling runtime decisions about remote memory access

For 128B reads, Host-Host achieves 19.4M reads/s while NIC-Host achieves 9.5M reads/s (49% of Host-Host)
In Bluefield-1, the round-trip time of 1-sided RDMA reads from another host is lower (2.7µs) than the RTT from the BF1 CPU (3.1µs) to its host memory

RMCs allow a constant amount of data transfer (24 bytes request, 8 bytes result) for linked list scans, while 1-sided operations transfer data proportional to list length

RMCs reduce the amount of bulk data transferred over the network fabric, reducing congestion
limitations: RMCs implemented on today's SmartNICs (BF1) would decrease network load but would not decrease delays compared to 1-sided operations
Host memory access latency, especially for small memory reads, is the main impediment to achieving the RMC vision on current hardware
Limited NIC resources will restrict the size (number of instructions) and runtime of RMCs
A complete RMC API specification and concrete programming model are left for future work
paper_profile.summary: This paper proposes Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), an extension to RDMA that allows applications to install customized 1-sided RDMA operations. RMCs are memory-oriented software procedures registered and invoked by a client and executed by a remote server's RDMA NIC CPUs, supporting operations such as reading/writing host memory, atomics, conditional branching, monitoring writes, and basic computation. The paper argues that forthcoming CPU-based SmartNICs (focusing on Mellanox Bluefield-1) will have the hardware capabilities to efficiently support RMCs, and provides a feasibility analysis covering PCIe bandwidth, NIC-to-host memory access latency, and RMC execution rate. The authors identify host memory access latency, especially for small reads, as the main current impediment, but project that faster CPUs, new IO busses, and software improvements will resolve this. They model two workloads (linked list scanning and remote buffer hashing) comparing RMCs to 1-sided RDMA, finding that RMCs reduce network load and congestion but on current BF1 hardware do not reduce latency; however, idealized future SmartNICs would yield decreased latency for workloads with repeated host memory accesses. The paper also discusses implementation challenges including low-cost memory isolation, preemption and scheduling, and programming language design, and analyzes tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided, and 2-sided operations, arguing that RMCs as an abstraction enable runtime decisions about remote memory access location.

paper_profile.title: Deep Learning with Differential Privacy
paper_profile.abstract: Machine learning techniques based on neural networks are achieving remarkable results in a wide variety of domains. Often, the training of models requires large, representative datasets, which may be crowdsourced and contain sensitive information. The models should not expose private information in these datasets. Addressing this goal, we develop new algorithmic techniques for learning and a refined analysis of privacy costs within the framework of differential privacy. Our implementation and experiments demonstrate that we can train deep neural networks with non-convex objectives, under a modest privacy budget, and at a manageable cost in software complexity, training efficiency, and model quality.
paper_profile.research_problem: How to train deep neural networks with non-convex objectives under a modest ("single-digit") differential privacy budget, providing rigorous privacy guarantees for models trained on sensitive crowdsourced datasets, while keeping costs in software complexity, training efficiency, and model quality manageable.
methods: Numerical integration for privacy loss moments
main_contributions: Demonstrates that tracking higher moments of the privacy loss yields much tighter estimates of overall privacy loss, both asymptotically and empirically

Demonstrates training deep neural networks with non-convex objectives under a modest privacy budget on MNIST and CIFAR-10

paper_profile.summary: This paper presents a framework for training deep neural networks with differential privacy guarantees. The authors develop a differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm that clips per-example gradient norms and adds Gaussian noise, combined with a new privacy accounting method called the moments accountant. The moments accountant tracks higher moments of the privacy loss random variable, providing tighter privacy bounds than the strong composition theorem—saving a sqrt(log(1/delta)) factor in epsilon and a Tq factor in delta. The approach is implemented in TensorFlow, including an efficient per-example gradient operator, a privacy accountant, and differentially private PCA. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that deep networks with non-convex objectives can be trained under modest ("single-digit") privacy budgets: on MNIST, 97% test accuracy is achieved with (8, 10^-5)-differential privacy, and on CIFAR-10, 73% accuracy with (8, 10^-5)-differential privacy. The paper also analyzes the effect of hyperparameters such as lot size, noise level, learning rate, clipping bound, PCA dimensions, and number of hidden units on accuracy under privacy constraints.

paper_profile.title: Defects4J: A Database of Existing Faults to Enable Controlled Testing Studies for Java Programs
paper_profile.abstract: Empirical studies in software testing research may not be comparable, reproducible, or characteristic of practice. One reason is that real bugs are too infrequently used in software testing research. Extracting and reproducing real bugs is challenging and as a result hand-seeded faults or mutants are commonly used as a substitute. This paper presents Defects4J, a database and extensible framework providing real bugs to enable reproducible studies in software testing research. The initial version of Defects4J contains 357 real bugs from 5 real-world open source programs. Each real bug is accompanied by a comprehensive test suite that can expose (demonstrate) that bug. Defects4J is extensible and builds on top of each program's version control system. Once a program is configured in Defects4J, new bugs can be added to the database with little or no effort. Defects4J features a framework to easily access faulty and fixed program versions and corresponding test suites. This framework also provides a high-level interface to common tasks in software testing research, making it easy to conduct and reproduce empirical studies. Defects4J is publicly available at http://defects4j.org.
paper_profile.research_problem: Empirical studies in software testing research are often not comparable, reproducible, or characteristic of practice because real bugs are too infrequently used, with hand-seeded faults or mutants commonly used as substitutes. The paper addresses the challenge of extracting, reproducing, and isolating real bugs from version control history to enable reproducible testing studies.

paper_profile.summary: This paper presents Defects4J, a database and extensible framework that provides real bugs to enable reproducible, controlled testing studies for Java programs. The initial version contains 357 real bugs from 5 large open source programs (JFreeChart, Closure Compiler, Commons Math, Joda-Time, Commons Lang). Each bug is accompanied by a comprehensive test suite with at least one test that exposes the bug (passes on the fixed version but fails on the faulty version). The paper describes a methodology for reproducing and isolating real bugs from version control history: automated identification of bug-fixing commits, automated reproduction by removing failing tests and executing suites on faulty versions, and manual review/isolation of bug fixes to exclude unrelated changes such as features or refactorings. Defects4J provides a database abstraction layer that abstracts heterogeneous version control and build systems, giving uniform access to faulty and fixed program versions and build targets. It also features a test execution framework with components for monitoring test execution, test suite manipulation, test generation (using EvoSuite), mutation analysis (using Major), and code coverage analysis (using Cobertura and CodeCover). The paper compares Defects4J to related work including SIR, iBugs, and the Siemens benchmark suite, highlighting advantages in number of real bugs, isolation of bugs, and the comprehensive test execution framework. Future work includes adding more programs and bugs and improving bug metadata with classification.

paper_profile.title: The Promises and Perils of Mining GitHub
paper_profile.abstract: With over 10 million git repositories, GitHub is becoming one of the most important source of software artifacts on the Internet. Researchers are starting to mine the information stored in GitHub's event logs, trying to understand how its users employ the site to collaborate on software. However, so far there have been no studies describing the quality and properties of the data available from GitHub. We document the results of an empirical study aimed at understanding the characteristics of the repositories in GitHub and how users take advantage of GitHub's main features—namely commits, pull requests, and issues. Our results indicate that, while GitHub is a rich source of data on software development, mining GitHub for research purposes should take various potential perils into consideration. We show, for example, that the majority of the projects are personal and inactive; that GitHub is also being used for free storage and as a Web hosting service; and that almost 40% of all pull requests do not appear as merged, even though they were. We provide a set of recommendations for software engineering researchers on how to approach the data in GitHub.

paper_profile.summary: This empirical study investigates the promises and perils of mining GitHub data for software engineering research. The authors used a mixed-methods approach combining an exploratory survey of 240 GitHub users, quantitative analysis of the GHTorrent dataset, and manual inspection of 434 randomly selected repositories. They identified nine perils: (I) a repository is not necessarily a project (forks must be aggregated with base repositories); (II) most projects have very few commits (median of 6); (III) most projects are inactive (46% inactive in the last six months); (IV) a large portion of repositories are not for software development (only 63.4% of the manual sample); (V) two thirds of projects are personal (71.6% of repositories); (VI) only a fraction of projects use pull requests and their use is skewed; (VII) GitHub records only reworked commits, not original ones, when pull requests are updated; (VIII) most pull requests appear as non-merged even when actually merged (only 37% merged via GitHub facilities, with heuristics identifying an extra 42%); and (IX) many active projects do not conduct all development in GitHub (23% of committers are not GitHub users). The paper also highlights two promises: GitHub provides valuable data for studying code reviews via pull requests, and the interlinking of developers, pull requests, issues, and commits provides a comprehensive view of development activities. The authors developed heuristics (H1-H4) to detect pull requests merged outside GitHub and provide recommendations for researchers on how to select appropriate projects and avoid biases, such as considering projects with a balance of commits and pull requests and more than 2 committers/authors.

paper_profile.title: node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks
paper_profile.abstract: Prediction tasks over nodes and edges in networks require careful effort in engineering features used by learning algorithms. Recent research in the broader field of representation learning has led to significant progress in automating prediction by learning the features themselves. However, present feature learning approaches are not expressive enough to capture the diversity of connectivity patterns observed in networks. Here we propose node2vec, an algorithmic framework for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks. In node2vec, we learn a mapping of nodes to a low-dimensional space of features that maximizes the likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods of nodes. We define a flexible notion of a node's network neighborhood and design a biased random walk procedure, which efficiently explores diverse neighborhoods. Our algorithm generalizes prior work which is based on rigid notions of network neighborhoods, and we argue that the added flexibility in exploring neighborhoods is the key to learning richer representations. We demonstrate the efficacy of node2vec over existing state-of-the-art techniques on multi-label classification and link prediction in several real-world networks from diverse domains. Taken together, our work represents a new way for efficiently learning state-of-the-art task-independent representations in complex networks.
paper_profile.research_problem: Learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks that capture the diversity of connectivity patterns, balancing homophily and structural equivalence, in a scalable and task-independent manner.

paper_profile.summary: The paper proposes node2vec, an algorithmic framework for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks. node2vec learns a mapping of nodes to a low-dimensional feature space that maximizes the likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods of nodes. The key contribution is a flexible notion of a node's network neighborhood, achieved through a family of biased 2nd order random walks governed by two parameters: the return parameter p and the in-out parameter q. These parameters allow the search to smoothly interpolate between breadth-first sampling (BFS), which captures structural equivalence, and depth-first sampling (DFS), which captures homophily. The objective is optimized using stochastic gradient descent with negative sampling, extending the Skip-gram architecture to networks. The paper also extends node features to edge features using simple binary operators (Average, Hadamard, Weighted-L1, Weighted-L2). Experiments on multi-label classification (BlogCatalog, PPI, Wikipedia) and link prediction (Facebook, PPI, arXiv ASTRO-PH) show node2vec outperforms state-of-the-art methods (DeepWalk, LINE, Spectral Clustering) by up to 26.7% on classification and 12.6% on link prediction. The algorithm is semi-supervised, robust to noisy or missing edges, and scales linearly to networks with millions of nodes in a few hours. The Hadamard operator is found to be the most stable for link prediction.

paper_profile.title: Good r-Divisions Imply Optimal Amortized Decremental Biconnectivity
paper_profile.abstract: We present a data structure that, given a graph G of n vertices and m edges, and a suitable pair of nested r-divisions of G, preprocesses G in O(m + n) time and handles any series of edge-deletions in O(m) total time while answering queries to pairwise biconnectivity in worst-case O(1) time. In case the vertices are not biconnected, the data structure can return a cutvertex separating them in worst-case O(1) time. As an immediate consequence, this gives optimal amortized decremental biconnectivity, 2-edge connectivity, and connectivity for large classes of graphs, including planar graphs and other minor free graphs.
paper_profile.research_problem: Whether decremental (deletion-only) connectivity, 2-edge connectivity, biconnectivity, or minimum cut for general graphs can be solved in amortized constant time per edge-deletion, or whether non-trivial lower bounds exist. The paper addresses maintaining biconnectivity, 2-edge connectivity, and connectivity under edge and vertex deletions for large classes of graphs including planar and minor-free graphs.

main_contributions: A data structure that, given a graph G and a suitable pair of nested r-divisions, preprocesses G in O(m+n) time and handles any series of edge-deletions in O(m) total time while answering pairwise biconnectivity queries in worst-case O(1) time.
The data structure can return a cutvertex separating non-biconnected vertices, specifically the nearest cutvertex, in worst-case O(1) time.

paper_profile.summary: The paper presents a data structure for decremental (deletion-only) biconnectivity. Given a graph G with n vertices and m edges and a suitable pair of nested r-divisions, the structure preprocesses G in O(m+n) time and handles any series of edge-deletions in O(m) total time while answering pairwise biconnectivity queries in worst-case O(1) time. For non-biconnected vertex pairs, it can return the nearest cutvertex separating them in O(1) time. The approach generalizes and improves upon the planar decremental connectivity result of Lacki and Sankowski, extending from planar graphs to r-divisible graphs and from plain connectivity to 2-edge connectivity and biconnectivity. The key technical tools are the compressed BC-forest (obtained from block-cutpoint trees by contracting paths between critical nodes), the patchwork graph (stitching compressed BC-forests of regions together via shared boundary vertices), and bicapacitated biconnectivity (viewing the BC-forest as a bicapacitated graph where non-bridge blocks have capacity 2). The structure uses nested r-divisions with three levels (top, middle, bottom), where bottom-level regions of polyloglog size are handled via look-up tables to achieve O(1) update and query time in the practical RAM model. Decremental changes are modeled by three operations: path deletions, block splits, and pseudoblock contractions, which are handled by a fully dynamic biconnectivity data structure. Nearest cutvertex queries are answered via characteristic ancestor queries on dynamic trees. As a consequence, the paper obtains optimal amortized decremental biconnectivity, 2-edge connectivity, and connectivity for planar, bounded genus, and minor-free graphs, with a linear-time algorithm for computing r-divisions in minor-free graphs. The question of whether the data structure generally admits vertex deletions in O(n) total time remains open.

paper_profile.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering
paper_profile.abstract: Radiance Field methods have recently revolutionized novel-view synthesis of scenes captured with multiple photos or videos. However, achieving high visual quality still requires neural networks that are costly to train and render, while recent faster methods inevitably trade off speed for quality. For unbounded and complete scenes (rather than isolated objects) and 1080p resolution rendering, no current method can achieve real-time display rates. We introduce three key elements that allow us to achieve state-of-the-art visual quality while maintaining competitive training times and importantly allow high-quality real-time (≥ 30 fps) novel-view synthesis at 1080p resolution. First, starting from sparse points produced during camera calibration, we represent the scene with 3D Gaussians that preserve desirable properties of continuous volumetric radiance fields for scene optimization while avoiding unnecessary computation in empty space; Second, we perform interleaved optimization/density control of the 3D Gaussians, notably optimizing anisotropic covariance to achieve an accurate representation of the scene; Third, we develop a fast visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting and both accelerates training and allows real-time rendering. We demonstrate state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering on several established datasets.

paper_profile.summary: This paper introduces 3D Gaussian Splatting, a method for real-time radiance field rendering that achieves state-of-the-art visual quality with competitive training times. The method represents scenes using a set of 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, each defined by position, opacity, anisotropic covariance, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Three key components are introduced: (1) 3D Gaussians as a flexible, explicit, differentiable volumetric scene representation that avoids computation in empty space; (2) interleaved optimization and adaptive density control (clone and split operations) that optimizes anisotropic covariance for accurate scene representation; and (3) a fast, visibility-aware, tile-based differentiable rasterizer using GPU radix sort that supports anisotropic splatting with alpha-blending and allows an unlimited number of splats to receive gradients. The method is evaluated on the Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, and synthetic Blender datasets. Results show quality on par with or slightly better than Mip-NeRF360 (the previous quality state-of-the-art) while achieving real-time rendering at 93-135 fps and training times of 35-45 minutes (compared to 48 hours for Mip-NeRF360). Ablations demonstrate the importance of SfM initialization, clone/split densification, anisotropic covariance, spherical harmonics, and unlimited gradient depth complexity. The authors note limitations including artifacts in poorly observed regions, popping artifacts, and higher memory consumption than NeRF-based solutions.

paper_profile.title: Conformer: Convolution-augmented Transformer for Speech Recognition
paper_profile.abstract: Recently Transformer and Convolution neural network (CNN) based models have shown promising results in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), outperforming Recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Transformer models are good at capturing content-based global interactions, while CNNs exploit local features effectively. In this work, we achieve the best of both worlds by studying how to combine convolution neural networks and transformers to model both local and global dependencies of an audio sequence in a parameter-efficient way. To this regard, we propose the convolution-augmented transformer for speech recognition, named Conformer. Conformer significantly outperforms the previous Transformer and CNN based models achieving state-of-the-art accuracies. On the widely used LibriSpeech benchmark, our model achieves WER of 2.1%/4.3% without using a language model and 1.9%/3.9% with an external language model on test/testother. We also observe competitive performance of 2.7%/6.3% with a small model of only 10M parameters.

paper_profile.summary: The paper introduces Conformer, a convolution-augmented Transformer architecture for end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The Conformer block consists of four stacked modules: a feed-forward module, a multi-headed self-attention module, a convolution module, and a second feed-forward module, arranged in a Macaron-style sandwich structure with half-step residual connections. The self-attention module uses relative sinusoidal positional encoding from Transformer-XL, while the convolution module uses a pointwise convolution with GLU gating, a 1-D depthwise convolution, batchnorm, and swish activation. The authors evaluate three model sizes (Conformer S/M/L with 10M, 30M, and 118M parameters) on the LibriSpeech benchmark. The large model achieves state-of-the-art WER of 2.1%/4.3% without a language model and 1.9%/3.9% with an external language model on test/testother. The medium model outperforms the previously published Transformer Transducer which uses 139M parameters. Extensive ablation studies examine the effects of the convolution block, Macaron-style feed-forward modules, relative positional embeddings, swish activation, attention head count, convolution kernel sizes, and different strategies for combining convolution and self-attention modules. The authors conclude that the convolution module is the most critical component, and that placing it after the self-attention module works best for speech recognition.

paper_profile.title: Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors
paper_profile.abstract: Memory isolation is a key property of a reliable and secure computing system — an access to one memory address should not have unintended side effects on data stored in other addresses. However, as DRAM process technology scales down to smaller dimensions, it becomes more difficult to prevent DRAM cells from electrically interacting with each other. In this paper, we expose the vulnerability of commodity DRAM chips to disturbance errors. By reading from the same address in DRAM, we show that it is possible to corrupt data in nearby addresses. More specifically, activating the same row in DRAM corrupts data in nearby rows. We demonstrate this phenomenon on Intel and AMD systems using a malicious program that generates many DRAM accesses. We induce errors in most DRAM modules (110 out of 129) from three major DRAM manufacturers. From this we conclude that many deployed systems are likely to be at risk. We identify the root cause of disturbance errors as the repeated toggling of a DRAM row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. We provide an extensive characterization study of disturbance errors and their behavior using an FPGA-based testing platform. Among our key findings, we show that (i) it takes as few as 139K accesses to induce an error and (ii) up to one in every 1.7K cells is susceptible to errors. After examining various potential ways of addressing the problem, we propose a low-overhead solution to prevent the errors.

paper_profile.summary: This paper exposes and characterizes DRAM disturbance errors (the "row hammer" phenomenon), where repeatedly activating the same DRAM row corrupts data in nearby rows, violating memory isolation. The authors demonstrate the phenomenon on real Intel (Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell) and AMD (Piledriver) systems using a user-level program that continuously reads from DRAM, inducing thousands of bit-flips. They identify the root cause as repeated toggling of a row's wordline, which stresses inter-cell coupling effects that accelerate charge leakage from nearby rows. Using an FPGA-based testing platform, they characterize 129 DDR3 DRAM modules (972 chips) from three major manufacturers, finding disturbance errors in 110 modules (836 chips), with all modules manufactured in 2012-2013 being vulnerable. Key findings include that as few as 139K activations can induce an error, up to one in 1.7K cells is disturbable, victim cells are predominantly localized to two adjacent rows of the aggressor row, and errors are mostly repeatable and weakly influenced by temperature. The paper examines seven potential solutions and proposes PARA (probabilistic adjacent row activation), a stateless low-overhead mechanism that refreshes adjacent rows with a small probability each time a row is opened and closed. PARA provides a strong statistical guarantee against disturbance errors (error probability of 9.4e-14 over one year with p=0.001 and Nth=100K) while incurring only 0.197% average performance degradation across 29 benchmarks.

paper_profile.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
paper_profile.abstract: Recent methods for learning vector space representations of words have succeeded in capturing fine-grained semantic and syntactic regularities using vector arithmetic, but the origin of these regularities has remained opaque. We analyze and make explicit the model properties needed for such regularities to emerge in word vectors. The result is a new global log-bilinear regression model that combines the advantages of the two major model families in the literature: global matrix factorization and local context window methods. Our model efficiently leverages statistical information by training only on the nonzero elements in a word-word co-occurrence matrix, rather than on the entire sparse matrix or on individual context windows in a large corpus. The model produces a vector space with meaningful substructure, as evidenced by its performance of 75% on a recent word analogy task. It also outperforms related models on similarity tasks and named entity recognition.

paper_profile.summary: The paper introduces GloVe (Global Vectors), a new global log-bilinear regression model for learning word vector representations. The authors analyze the model properties needed for linear semantic and syntactic regularities to emerge in word vectors, arguing that ratios of co-occurrence probabilities are the appropriate starting point. They derive a weighted least squares objective that trains only on the nonzero elements of a word-word co-occurrence matrix, combining the advantages of global matrix factorization methods (like LSA) and local context window methods (like skip-gram). The model uses a weighting function f(x) with parameters xmax=100 and alpha=3/4, trained with AdaGrad. The paper shows the relationship between GloVe and skip-gram/ivLBL models, and provides a complexity analysis showing the model scales as O(|C|^0.8) under a power-law assumption. Experiments on the word analogy task (75% accuracy on a 42B token corpus), five word similarity tasks, and the CoNLL-2003 NER benchmark show GloVe outperforms other models including word2vec, SVD baselines, HPCA, HSMN, and CW. The paper also analyzes the effects of vector length, context window size/type, corpus size, and training time on performance.

paper_profile.title: Deep Kernel Learning
paper_profile.abstract: We introduce scalable deep kernels, which combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods. Specifically, we transform the inputs of a spectral mixture base kernel with a deep architecture, using local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and structure exploiting (Kronecker and Toeplitz) algebra for a scalable kernel representation. These closed-form kernels can be used as drop-in replacements for standard kernels, with benefits in expressive power and scalability. We jointly learn the properties of these kernels through the marginal likelihood of a Gaussian process. Inference and learning cost O(n) for n training points, and predictions cost O(1) per test point. On a large and diverse collection of applications, including a dataset with 2 million examples, we show improved performance over scalable Gaussian processes with flexible kernel learning models, and stand-alone deep architectures.

paper_profile.summary: The paper introduces scalable deep kernels that combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods. The authors transform the inputs of a base kernel (RBF or spectral mixture) with a deep feedforward or convolutional architecture, then use local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and Kronecker/Toeplitz structure exploiting algebra (via the KISS-GP approximation) to create scalable closed-form covariance kernels for Gaussian processes. All deep kernel hyperparameters (network weights and base kernel parameters) are learned jointly by backpropagating derivatives through the Gaussian process marginal likelihood, without approximate Bayesian inference. The resulting model effectively has a hidden layer with an infinite number of adaptive basis functions, achieving O(n) training cost and O(1) per-test-point prediction cost. Experiments on a wide range of UCI regression datasets (including a 2-million-example dataset), Olivetti face orientation extraction, MNIST digit magnitude extraction, and step function recovery show that DKL consistently outperforms scalable Gaussian processes with expressive kernels, stand-alone deep neural networks, and GPs applied to the outputs of trained deep networks. The spectral mixture base kernel provides notable additional performance gains over RBF, and the learned kernels reveal interpretable structure (e.g., faces with similar rotation angles become highly correlated). The approach also naturally produces posterior predictive distributions, useful for applications such as reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization.

paper_profile.title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
paper_profile.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) frame opportunities and challenges for user interface design. Principles for human-AI interaction have been discussed in the human-computer interaction community for over two decades, but more study and innovation are needed in light of advances in AI and the growing uses of AI technologies in human-facing applications. We propose 18 generally applicable design guidelines for human-AI interaction. These guidelines are validated through multiple rounds of evaluation including a user study with 49 design practitioners who tested the guidelines against 20 popular AI-infused products. The results verify the relevance of the guidelines over a spectrum of interaction scenarios and reveal gaps in our knowledge, highlighting opportunities for further research. Based on the evaluations, we believe the set of design guidelines can serve as a resource to practitioners working on the design of applications and features that harness AI technologies, and to researchers interested in the further development of guidelines for human-AI interaction design.

paper_profile.summary: This CHI 2019 paper proposes and validates 18 generally applicable design guidelines for human-AI interaction. The authors synthesized over 150 AI-related design recommendations from academic and industry sources into a set of guidelines organized into four temporal categories: "Initially" (G1-G2), "During interaction" (G3-G6), "When wrong" (G7-G11), and "Over time" (G12-G18). The guidelines were developed and refined through a four-phase process: (1) consolidating guidelines from industry products, public articles, and scholarly papers via affinity diagramming; (2) an internal modified heuristic evaluation that reduced the set from 20 to 18 guidelines; (3) a user study with 49 HCI practitioners who tested the guidelines against 20 popular AI-infused products across 10 categories; and (4) an expert evaluation of the revisions with 11 experts. The user study found 785 examples of the guidelines (313 applications, 277 violations, 89 neutrals, 106 "does not apply"), demonstrating broad relevance across product categories. Key findings include that explanation-related guidelines (G11) had high violation counts, guidelines on social norms and biases (G5, G6) were least clear and most often rated "does not apply," and voice assistants had the most "does not apply" instances. The authors discuss trade-offs between generality and specialization, note limitations for non-GUI systems and high-risk domains, and highlight the need for diverse evaluators to recognize social norms and biases.

paper_profile.title: Slide Rule: Making Mobile Touch Screens Accessible to Blind People Using Multi-Touch Interaction Techniques
paper_profile.abstract: Recent advances in touch screen technology have increased the prevalence of touch screens and have prompted a wave of new touch screen-based devices. However, touch screens are still largely inaccessible to blind users, who must adopt error-prone compensatory strategies to use them or find accessible alternatives. This inaccessibility is due to interaction techniques that require the user to visually locate objects on the screen. To address this problem, we introduce Slide Rule, a set of audio-based multi-touch interaction techniques that enable blind users to access touch screen applications. We describe the design of Slide Rule, our interaction techniques, and a user study in which 10 blind people used Slide Rule and a button-based Pocket PC screen reader. Results show that Slide Rule was significantly faster than the button-based system, and was preferred by 7 of 10 users. However, users made more errors when using Slide Rule than when using the more familiar button-based system.

paper_profile.summary: The paper introduces Slide Rule, a set of audio-based multi-touch interaction techniques that make touch screen mobile devices accessible to blind users. Slide Rule provides a completely non-visual interface that repurposes a touch screen as a talking touch-sensitive surface, requiring only a standard multi-touch screen and audio output with no additional hardware. It uses four basic gesture interactions: a one-finger scan to browse lists, a second-finger tap to select items, a multi-directional flick for additional actions, and an L-select gesture for browsing hierarchical information, plus a double-tap gesture. The design was informed by formative interviews with 8 blind mobile device users and iterative prototyping with 3 blind users, guided by design principles including risk-free exploration, finger-resolution operation, reduced selection accuracy demands, quick browsing, intuitive gestural mappings, and the ability to query location and return home. The techniques were implemented in three prototype applications (Phone, Mail, Music) on an Apple iPhone. A user study with 10 blind participants compared Slide Rule against a button-based Pocket PC running Mobile Speak Pocket. Results showed Slide Rule was significantly faster (11.69s vs 12.79s mean task time), with significantly lower listening time per item, and was preferred by 7 of 10 participants. However, users made more errors with Slide Rule (0.20 errors per trial vs none for the Pocket PC), reflecting a speed-accuracy tradeoff. Questionnaire results showed the Pocket PC was rated significantly higher on ease of use, feeling in control, ease of learning, and familiarity, yet participants still preferred Slide Rule. The paper discusses design implications, the cost of errors, and future work including composite interaction techniques, text entry methods, support for larger displays, and applicability to sighted users in eyes-free contexts.

paper_profile.title: LINE: Large-scale Information Network Embedding
paper_profile.abstract: This paper studies the problem of embedding very large information networks into low-dimensional vector spaces, which is useful in many tasks such as visualization, node classification, and link prediction. Most existing graph embedding methods do not scale for real world information networks which usually contain millions of nodes. In this paper, we propose a novel network embedding method called the "LINE," which is suitable for arbitrary types of information networks: undirected, directed, and/or weighted. The method optimizes a carefully designed objective function that preserves both the local and global network structures. An edge-sampling algorithm is proposed that addresses the limitation of the classical stochastic gradient descent and improves both the effectiveness and the efficiency of the inference. Empirical experiments prove the effectiveness of the LINE on a variety of real-world information networks, including language networks, social networks, and citation networks. The algorithm is very efficient, which is able to learn the embedding of a network with millions of vertices and billions of edges in a few hours on a typical single machine.

paper_profile.summary: The paper proposes LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding), a network embedding model that maps vertices of very large information networks into low-dimensional vector spaces. LINE defines and preserves two complementary notions of proximity: first-order proximity (local pairwise proximity captured by observed edge weights) and second-order proximity (similarity of neighborhood structures, capturing shared neighbors). The model uses carefully designed objective functions for each proximity, optimized via negative sampling and asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. A key contribution is an edge-sampling algorithm using an alias table that samples edges proportional to their weights and treats them as binary edges, addressing the gradient explosion problem caused by high variance in edge weights. The overall time complexity is O(dK|E|), linear in the number of edges. The paper also discusses handling low-degree vertices (via adding second-order neighbors) and new vertices. Experiments on language (Wikipedia), social (Flickr, Youtube), and citation (DBLP) networks evaluate word analogy, document classification, and multi-label node classification. Results show LINE(2nd) outperforms baselines including graph factorization, DeepWalk, and SkipGram on word analogy; LINE(1st+2nd) significantly outperforms all methods on classification tasks; and LINE is efficient, processing networks with millions of nodes and billions of edges in a few hours on a single machine. The paper also analyzes performance with respect to network sparsity, parameter sensitivity, and scalability with multiple threads.

paper_profile.title: Trajectory-based Social Circle Inference
paper_profile.abstract: Learning explicit and implicit patterns in human trajectories plays an important role in many Location-Based Social Networks (LBSNs) applications, such as trajectory classification (e.g., walking, driving, etc.), trajectory-user linking, friend recommendation, etc. A particular problem that has attracted much attention recently – and is the focus of our work – is the Trajectory-based Social Circle Inference (TSCI), aiming at inferring user social circles (mainly social friendship) based on motion trajectories and without any explicit social networked information. Existing approaches addressing TSCI lack satisfactory results due to the challenges related to data sparsity, accessibility and model efficiency. Motivated by the recent success of machine learning in trajectory mining, in this paper we formulate TSCI as a novel multi-label classification problem and develop a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)-based framework called DeepTSCI to use human mobility patterns for inferring corresponding social circles. We propose three methods to learn the latent representations of trajectories, based on: (1) bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM); (2) Autoencoder; and (3) Variational autoencoder. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed methods perform well and achieve significant improvement in terms of macro-R, macro-F1 and accuracy when compared to baselines.

paper_profile.summary: The paper addresses Trajectory-based Social Circle Inference (TSCI), the problem of inferring users' social circles (friendships) based purely on their motion trajectories without any explicit social network information. The authors formulate TSCI as a multi-label classification problem and propose DeepTSCI, an RNN-based framework with three variants: DeepTSCI-LSTM/Bi-DeepTSCI (using LSTM and bidirectional LSTM), DeepTSCI-AE (using autoencoder pre-training), and DeepTSCI-VAE (using variational autoencoder). The framework embeds check-ins into low-dimensional vectors via CBOW with hierarchical softmax, splits trajectories into sub-trajectories, and uses a Friend Decoder multi-label classifier to predict friendship sets. Two subtasks are studied: RT-TSCI (predicting friends for existing users) and RU-TSCI (predicting friends for new users). Experiments on Brightkite, Gowalla, and Foursquare (Tokyo and New York) datasets show that DeepTSCI-VAE achieves the best performance across macro-R, macro-F1, and accuracy compared to baselines including Co-Visit, MF, Decision Trees, SVM, RandomForest, MLP, TULER, and DeepMIML. The authors note that RU-TSCI performance is relatively low due to a cold-start-like problem. Future work includes incorporating semantic inter-relationships among friends and reinforcement learning methods.
